title: Lina and the Flying Scores
markdown:
The Sunny Meadow Summer Games were quite the grand event. Every year, when the sun warmed the meadows just so and buttercups glowed like tiny golden coins, the creatures gathered for friendly fun. And who was always there, nestled by the finish line with a neat stack of colourful cards and a very important quill? Lina the otter. Lina loved things perfectly tidy. She had a special booth of smooth river stones and soft green moss, everything organised with the neatness only an otter's clever paws could manage. Her favourite quill, tipped with a feather from a particularly chatty jay, waited patiently.

This year's most exciting event was the Comic Relay. Not the fastest — the funniest. As the whistle blew, a clear sharp note through the hum of bees, the first runner, Tegwen Bear, lumbered off. He wasn't just running; he was doing a little jig, a happy wobble, and a grand sweeping wave that made everyone giggle until their tummies ached. Lina, with a gentle puff, marked her first card: +1 for Jig, +1 for Wiggle, +1 for Wave. Quill steady.

Next, Flora Fox, sleek as a dart. Flora never just ran. She pirouetted at the halfway mark, red fur swirling, then leapt over an imaginary puddle with a flourish and a flick of her magnificent tail. Lina's quill scratched: +1 for Pirouette, +1 for Leap, +1 for Tail Flick. Bonus points, she liked to think, for bravery and beauty.

Here's the thing: all those flourishes didn't slow anyone down. Not one bit. They just made the race more fun to watch. Spectators from field mice to storks roared and cheered. Lina tried her very best to score every single one. Her pile of cards grew, each a different hue.

Then Bert the goat. Bert wasn't known for quiet grace. He bounced. Bounded. Pranced. Hooves clippity-clop. And every so often, when particularly joyful, a tremendously happy "Baaa-ha-ha!" like a giggle mixed with a sneeze. Lina's brow furrowed. She chewed the quill, a habit for complications. +1 for Bounce, +1 for Prance, +1 for… joyful Baaa-ha-ha. A bit much, even for Lina. Her tidy tower of cards now leaned, threatening to spill.

And what do you suppose happened next? As Bert finished his spectacular bouncing run, a playful gust — dandelion seeds and the promise of rain — swept the meadow. Not a grumpy wind. A light mischievous one that ruffled grasses and made bluebells nod. It caught Lina's prize-winning scorecards. Careful tallies, neat marks, colourful cards — up like a flock of startled butterflies.

Lina gasped. Whiskers quivered. Heart thumped. All her hard work, gone in a blink. A yellow card with Tegwen's jig fluttered near the tallest oak. A pink one with Flora's pirouette spiralled toward the berry bushes. Paper rustled. The wind sighed.

But the curious thing about Sunny Meadow: when something unexpected happens, the creatures don't always frown. Coach Pippin, the wise old owl on the highest oak, hooted softly, a chuckle without a speech.

The runners didn't complain. Tegwen Bear used his big gentle paws to nudge colourful cards toward Lina's booth. Flora, with a graceful sweep of tail, gathered a few near her. Bert bounced and leaped not to win, but to bat tumbling cards in gentle arcs back toward the booth. Other animals joined in, chasing airborne colours, laughter echoing.

Lina, at first, darted her paws out to catch them. Soon she realised something wonderful: the wind wasn't destroying her scores; it was sharing them. Cards landed near happy faces. Yellow ones, dotted with Bert's paw prints and a smudge of grass, near giggling younger rabbits. Soft blue ones, Flora's elegant scribbles and a scent of wildflowers, to thoughtful badgers.

When the last card settled, there were no neat piles, no precise totals. There were smiles. Lots. Bert nudged a bright orange card toward Lina. "That one," he bleated, "was for my extra-special landing!" Smudged with grass and a cheerful print. Not perfect by Lina's old standards. Joyful.

Coach Pippin glided down. "Ah, Lina." He gestured at the happy scene. "The smiles are doing a good deal of the counting today."

Lina looked around, paws sticky with flower petals from gathering. She picked up a crumpled green card, a little damp with dew. Not a score anymore, not really. A memory of a playful wind, a bouncing goat, a meadow full of fun.

She wondered, lining the cards into a messy rainbow instead of a tower, whether next year she would score the jigs at all — or only keep a single card that said, simply, everyone laughed, which, as tallies went, was the hardest to lose in the wind.
